startup.name: Hub Labs
startup.one_liner: Deployment and data infrastructure for Embodied AI.
startup.description: Hub deploys hardware and embodied machines to collect data for robotics labs, and puts the same machines to work producing labor output for real world businesses. Customers are robotics labs that buy data and businesses that buy work. Team of about 50, San Francisco, Spring 2026.

yc_acceptance.basis: Blind test: the company is already accepted to YC for its batch, so the acceptance estimate is a placeholder near certainty rather than a forecast. The unconditional prior for a random applicant is about 1 percent (0.6 to 2 percent, third party figures in yc_acceptance.md).
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: Not applicable in this test because the company was accepted. Had it been assessed as an applicant, the most plausible reason for a no would be a crowded robot data narrative and unclear defensibility of a hardware and services mix. The founders would also need to show in the interview that they can ship quickly and have a specific first customer in mind, since YC weighs team speed and clear user need over market size.

ladder.why_it_fails: A round above 500K is the most likely outcome, so the main stopper is that the unit of work does not scale. If the machines are costly, break often or the data labs buy is not clearly better than teleoperation firms and public datasets, labs will pilot and not commit. A seed would also fail if investors see a services business with hardware margins.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series A requires proof that the labor output business and the data business are one flywheel and not two half businesses. The likely miss is utilisation: robots sit idle, customers pay per task below cost, and investors see robotics capex with services margins. Yondu and DeepAware show hardware teams stalling at seed with no verified A.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series B needs repeatable deployments with gross margin, not pilots. The likely stop is that a few frontier labs are the only data buyers and bring their own collection, while the real world labor customers churn after pilots. Capital intensity then forces a down round or a strategic sale instead of a clean B.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series C needs a fleet with contracted revenue, which almost no robotics company reaches within seven years. The likely stop is a plateau in which robot hardware commoditises, robot makers integrate data collection themselves, and the company becomes a service shop acquired for its fleet and contracts.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely the company stalls as a capital hungry services and hardware hybrid. Robotics lab demand for data is real but concentrated in a handful of buyers, who can build collection in house, and the labor side needs reliable robots that do not yet exist. Analogs such as Yondu and DeepAware show recent robotics companies with no verified round beyond seed, and exits at this stage are usually small acquisitions of fleets and teams.

killers.risk: Hardware and services margins make the business look unscalable to Series A investors.
killers.evidence: Robotics seed companies in the 2023 to 2025 cohort reach A at 8 percent (n=16) versus 22 percent for B2B overall.
killers.mitigation: Show contribution margin per deployed robot and a utilisation figure before raising A.

killers.risk: Data buyers are few and can collect in house, so the data line stays small.
killers.evidence: Robot data sellers multiplied in 2025 to 2026 and each depends on a handful of lab customers.
killers.mitigation: Lock multi year data contracts with two or three labs and keep the labor line as a second customer base.

killers.risk: The company tries to run two businesses at once with 50 people and splits focus.
killers.evidence: A team of 50 at batch start burns fast and needs proof on both revenue lines.
killers.mitigation: Choose the lead business by month six and use the other as support.

brand.rationale: Hub Labs is a common descriptor pair with little distinctiveness, but names of this type have not blocked B2B infrastructure companies in the YC data. The name should neither raise nor lower the ladder.

narrative.headline: A well staffed embodied AI data and labor company that likely raises a real seed and then faces the capital intensity wall.
narrative.general_summary: Hub Labs sells robot data to labs and robot labor to businesses. With about 50 people at batch start it is far larger than a typical YC team, which makes a seed above the standard deal very likely. The harder steps are Series A and B, because hardware and services margins make investors cautious: recent robotics cohorts reach A at under 10 percent known, and Yondu, DeepAware and Vassar show seed stage stalls. Upside comes from the unusual demand for robot data, which gives a strong fundraising window if utilisation and data quality are proven.

assumptions: Team size of 50 is taken at face value; it may include contractors or operators.

Blind test: only the batch input file and market web searches were used; no company specific records. The seed step is read as a round above the standard YC deal of about 500K dollars within roughly 12 months of batch start.

Extraction coverage is 662 of 6,399 companies researched in the calibration sample, plus recent cohort records; later cohorts are right censored, so base rates for 2023 to 2025 batches understate eventual progress.
